practice.title: Working with Desire
agreedSteps: Pick one practice from the spectrum and work with it over the next two weeks: (1) see that happiness comes from within, not from external objects; (2) find happiness from your love and compassion, recognizing the good feeling is coming from your own mind; (3) offer small pleasures to Buddha or Je Tsongkhapa at your heart; or (4) offer enjoyments to the self-generation.

Whichever level you choose, connect it to some understanding of emptiness — either by acknowledging the good feeling is coming from within, or by recognizing that the thing you find attractive is a creation of your own mind.
steps: Understand your desire better. Ask yourself honestly: what do I really desire right now? What does it feel like to follow that desire? What does it feel like to resist a non-virtuous desire? What does it feel like to do something virtuous but not want to be doing it?
When enjoying small pleasures — a cup of tea, a sunset, a beautiful sound — try offering unowned things to Buddha throughout the day. Just take beautiful things you encounter and mentally offer them.

If you have a tantric practice, experiment with taking a small pleasurable experience, offering it to Buddha at your heart or the self-generation, getting even a small blissful feeling, and then resting in whatever understanding of emptiness you have — even for one second.
practice.quote: Just take little, small pleasures and offer them to the guru at your heart or yourself as a self-generation. Just like a little cup of tea.

commentary.title: Lamrim Grounds Us and Makes Everything Light
content: Many people's emotional problems just come because they don't actually meditate on the Lamrim. If they just meditated on the Lamrim, they wouldn't have those emotional problems. All the heaviness and intensity in people's lives is usually based on one-life thinking. If you just stop doing that, almost all of it goes away — 99% of all the intensity and angst and worry. Poof. Make that go away and we have a huge burden lifted, and then we become an actual Buddhist.

When we do the Lamrim with the New Meditation Handbook, the Lamrim topics become like friends who walk with us all day — precious human life, death, karma — reminding us of the correct view of everything. And the correct view is much lighter than the ordinary view. The grounding gives us lightness, not heaviness.

commentary.title: The Actual Object of Lamrim Meditation
content: Our mind creates models of reality — it's never seen the truth, it's always just creating a model based on our biases and preferences and imperfect memory. It's very easy to do this with the Dharma. We rely on our imperfect memory which is modeling what we want to be there or what we imperfectly recall. Having the New Meditation Handbook and eventually memorizing verbatim important Dharma texts prevents this. The main object of each Lamrim meditation is marked clearly in the handbook.

The Lamrim is like eggplant parmesan. The main object is the whole dish. Joyful Path teaches us how to make the bread really well, the sauce really well, the cheese just right. We can zoom in on the component parts, but we're never making the sauce for the sauce's sake. It's part of a whole. We always want to come back to the whole.

commentary.title: Don't Over-Correct Your Practice Structure
content: When our mind goes a little funny despite having a good structure, the answer isn't always to add more scaffolding. Sometimes the takeaway is just: it takes time to reverse my karma. When we have a really good setup and we're doing everything right, it doesn't mean our karma will be instantly reformatted. We're still going to get weird minds, distracted minds, angry minds. Sometimes the answer is just: be patient with myself and keep up my structure.

Over-correcting in our Dharma practice can be a really bad habit. We try to create a structure based on our karma and our life, but once it feels pretty good, we try to let that ride and not over-correct. If we keep tearing things down that we set up, we never build the deep habits that can last decades — the ones that are fused in our mind. That's what we really want.

commentary.title: The Reverse Hockey Stick
content: When our practice starts to decline, it can look subtle at first, but that subtle movement implies something that involves a free fall. It's a reverse hockey stick. And it's different from the normal ups and downs of practice, which are just normal oscillations. The key skill is learning to distinguish between a normal undulation and a pattern — momentum building in an unhelpful direction. Usually we have to go through the full decline a few times before we build the skill to catch the cues early.

commentary.title: Three Scopes Oppose Three Types of Attachment
content: The three scopes of the Lamrim oppose three types of attachment. Meditations 1 through 5 oppose attachment to happiness in this life. The sixth meditation, renunciation, opposes attachment to happiness in future lives or in samsara generally. And meditations 7 through 21 oppose attachment to attaining spiritual realizations or enlightenment for our self alone.

Many people who study Buddhism deeply still get the relationship with attachment wrong, settling for something either ascetic or indulgent. Both are wrong, completely. Asceticism is abandoning objects of desire externally while still harboring attachment in our heart. Indulgence is looking for happiness outside of ourself. Both are insufficient tools — they lack an understanding of emptiness, which cuts through either extreme.

commentary.title: Desire Is Not the Enemy
content: Aspiration, desire, wish — they're all synonymous. There are virtuous desires, neutral desires, and non-virtuous desires. Desire by no means is the enemy. Attachment is the enemy. But pleasure is not the enemy. Pleasurable feelings are not the enemy. Attachment is.

Attachment is identifying a contaminated object, viewing it as a source of happiness, and then wishing for it. That's after ignorance the most important enemy to destroy. But it's important to distinguish attachment from desire and from pleasurable feeling itself — they are not the same thing at all.

commentary.title: The Four Levels of Transforming Enjoyments
content: There is a spectrum for learning to transform our enjoyments into the spiritual path. Level one is renunciation: simply starting to see that our happiness is within the mind. Level two is finding happiness and even bliss from our love and compassion — not from other people, but from our love for them. Other people can't make me happy, but my love for them can.

Level three is offering the pleasure of enjoying any object of desire to Buddha at our heart. We walk around all day and enjoy a coffee, a sunset, a beautiful song, and offer that pleasure to Je Tsongkhapa or Buddha at our heart. Level four is offering it to ourself as the self-generation. Because the self-generation is the synthesis of all Buddhas, when we offer enjoyments to it, we're making an offering to all Buddhas. This is a million-for-one deal: we simultaneously subtract the cause that binds us to samsara and create a ton of merit.

In the root tantra of Heruka, Vajradhara says: Making offerings to our self becomes an offering to all Buddhas. If we maintain awareness, whatever we enjoy becomes an offering to the deity. This is one of the things we explicitly vow to do in highest yoga tantra empowerment: enjoy objects of desire as offerings to the self-generation. Not avoid — enjoy.
commentary.quote: Other people can't make me happy, but my love for them can.

commentary.title: Pleasure, Emptiness, and the Blissful Mind
content: Whenever we're experiencing changing suffering, we're viewing the pleasure as coming from without. If we're 100% viewing the pleasure as coming from within the mind, we're basically meditating on emptiness. Coming from the mind, merely imputed, empty — are all synonyms. So if we have a pleasurable feeling and we're viewing it as merely imputed, that is a beautiful, virtuous mind leading us out of samsara.

This is why the practice must always connect to some understanding of emptiness. Without that connection, it's just enjoying worldly pleasure. It's only when we think 'this is merely imputed' or 'this is coming from the mind' that it becomes a Buddhist teaching. We have to very consciously make that recognition.

In sutra, we develop bodhichitta because that's the best sutra mind that mixes with emptiness. But in tantra, it's the blissful mind that mixes best with emptiness. So whenever we get even a small blissful feeling, we do a little meditation on emptiness. Even one second. The more we do this, the more we realize: every time I meditate on emptiness, this is how I want to do it.
